label: Paulin J. Hountondji
context: Edits a collaborative research programme originating in a 1987 Cotonou seminar.
works: Endogenous Knowledge: Research Trails (1997)

label: Pierre G. Mêtinhoué
context: Connects oral-source criticism, archaeology and material-culture history in the editor’s account.
works: The Study of Traditional Techniques and Know-how: Methodological Issues (1997)

label: Rodney Hilton
context: A British interlocutor who reads Bloch and Duby productively while contesting specific emphases on rebellion and crisis; his inclusion records exchange, not Annales membership.
works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

label: Jean-Philippe Genet
context: Appreciates Hilton’s peasant inquiry but questions period differentiation and treatment of the changing state; a particular review rather than a uniform Annales position.
works: Review of Hilton’s Les mouvements paysans du Moyen Âge (1980), p. 1069

label: Anton Blok
context: Questions the social-bandit model through power and patronage. Hobsbawm’s later response acknowledges this objection; Blok’s full original article remains unread.
works: “The Peasant and the Brigand: Social Banditry Reconsidered” (1972); response in Hobsbawm, Bandits, revised edition (2000)

label: Ludwig Wittgenstein
context: Geertz explicitly invokes later Wittgenstein when explaining public meaning. That selective use does not make all interpretive anthropology Wittgensteinian.
works: Philosophical Investigations (1953); Geertz, Thick Description (1973), pp. 12–13

label: Gilbert Ryle
context: Geertz adapts the distinction between outwardly similar actions with different meanings. Ryle’s philosophical lecture has its own inquiry into thinking and accomplishment.
works: The Thinking of Thoughts (1968); Geertz, Thick Description (1973), pp. 5–7

label: Stevan Harrell
context: Edits comparative local population studies; his later review questions broad inference from uneven evidence.
works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); retrospective review of Lee/Wang (2003)

label: W. E. B. Du Bois
context: Gilroy explicitly takes up double consciousness as a conceptual resource.
works: The Souls of Black Folk (1903)

label: Thomas Carlyle
context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

label: Lytton Strachey
context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

label: Dorothy Thompson
context: Uses a female sovereign to examine gender and power in a society restricting women’s political participation; a contemporary reviewer challenges parts of the causal argument.
works: Queen Victoria: Gender and Power (1990)

label: David Cannadine
context: Questions how convincingly Dorothy Thompson connects a female monarch with changes in women’s rights and republicanism; this is a particular review, not a neutral verdict on the whole book.
works: “The Ruling Exception” (1990), review of Queen Victoria: Gender and Power

label: Helen Maud Cam
context: Her memoir of Maitland interprets a historian’s scholarship and methods; this is distinct from her medieval institutional research.
works: Memoir prefacing Selected Historical Essays of F. W. Maitland (1957)

label: Hedwig Brühl
context: Mediates the 1877 commission for Delbrück to complete Pertz’s Gneisenau biography, in his retrospective account.
works: Gneisenau biography commission (1877), recalled in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

label: Georg Heinrich Pertz
context: His unfinished Gneisenau biography supplies the project Delbrück continues; archival biography becomes a route into wider critical war history.
works: Gneisenau biography, completed by Delbrück after the 1877 commission

label: Plutarch
context: Uses minor acts and a portrait analogy to explain a life’s selective treatment of character. One ancient practice, not the origin or entirety of biography.
works: Alexander, opening paragraph; archive translation credited to Dryden

label: James Boswell
context: Interweaves letters, recollected conversations and narrative, explicitly adapting Mason’s example. Claims candid portrayal rather than pure praise; actual completeness is not established by that claim.
works: Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Osgood abridgment (1917)

label: Sue Bailey Thurman
context: Participates in the WCWA Black women’s archives committee and presses for a separate archive; inclusion and authority are contested.
works: Black women’s archival work and the WCWA encounter, discussed by Voss-Hubbard (1995), citing Bettye Collier-Thomas (1986)

label: Mary McLeod Bethune
context: Her NCNW cooperates with WCWA after she declines the proposed committee chair; Black women’s preservation work exceeds this short-lived collaboration.
works: Black women’s archival work and the WCWA encounter, discussed by Voss-Hubbard (1995), citing Bettye Collier-Thomas (1986)

label: Mary Church Terrell
context: Terrell’s preserved papers are among the resources Rupp identifies in Flexner’s bibliography. This is a documentary contribution, not a claim of personal advice to Flexner.
works: Mary Church Terrell papers at the Library of Congress, cited by Flexner and discussed by Rupp (1992), p. 163

label: Roy Porter
context: Co-edits a collection spanning household economies, material objects, knowledge and design; his chapter asks about consumption as a disease of consumer society.
works: With John Brewer, ed., Consumption and the World of Goods (1993)

label: Julia Cherry Spruill
context: Examines dwellings, utensils, clothing and possible reading as evidence; prescriptive books are not transparent records of actual behavior.
works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938), chapters discussed and p. 208 quoted by Richter (1999)

label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
context: Everyday household materials and changing work offer an earlier comparison with consumption inquiry, without a claim that she founded its later movement.
works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; “History in a Back Yard” (1915), institutionally documented

label: Carole Shammas
context: Her comparison of goods’ values and wealth challenges interpretation of ownership frequencies; Weatherill acknowledges the problem.
works: The Pre-industrial Consumer in England and America (1990), through Weatherill’s1996 preface

label: Ernst Gombrich
context: Skinner and Dunn explicitly draw on problems of perceptual expectations and interpretation. This is a specified resource, not evidence that all contextual historians adopted Gombrich’s art history.
works: Art and Illusion (1960), cited by Skinner (1969), p. 7, and Dunn (1968), notes

label: Thomas Kuhn
context: Skinner invokes the priority of paradigms in interpreting evidence; Dunn also acknowledges the work among methodological resources.
works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), chapter V, reception in Skinner (1969), p. 7

label: Louis Marin
context: Chartier uses Marin’s analysis of signs and representation in examining the relation between absent objects, present images and conventions of recognition.
works: La critique du discours: Étude sur la Logique de Port-Royal et les Pensées de Pascal (1975), discussed by Chartier (1989)

label: Paul Ricœur
context: The meeting of text and reader supplies Chartier a resource; he also differentiates historically situated appropriation from a universal account of self-understanding.
works: Temps et récit, vol. III, Le temps raconté (1985), pp. 228–263 as cited by Chartier (1989)

label: Patricia O’Brien
context: Examines historical uses of Foucault. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
works: Michel Foucault’s History of Culture, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

label: Patrick Geary
context: Studies contested authentication and the narratives accompanying transferred relics.
works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),186–190

label: Jack A. Goldstone
context: Uses population change in a comparative explanation of state crises; a political-sociology application, distinct from household reconstruction.
works: Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (1991)

label: Louise A. Tilly
context: Joint work joins family history to questions about productive work and historical change.
works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975); Women, Work, and Family (1978)

label: Joan Wallach Scott
context: Joint work joins family history to questions about productive work and historical change.
works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975); Women, Work, and Family (1978)

label: Karl Julius Beloch
context: Ancient population estimates supply a concrete earlier resource for Delbrück’s military source criticism; distinct from later family reconstitution.
works: Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886), acknowledged by Delbrück

label: Henri Pirenne
context: Comparative and economic historian in dialogue with the founders.
works: “De la méthode comparative en histoire” (1923)

label: Rodney Hilton
context: Comparative peasant movements join production, conflict, political organization and belief; outcomes and evidence differ across periods. Acknowledges Bloch while criticizing particular Power and Duby emphases.
works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

label: M. M. Postan
context: His 1963 preface identifies editorial reconstruction of Power’s unfinished material; it distinguishes her draft from the published wording.
works: Preface to the tenth edition of Power, Medieval People (1963)

label: G. G. Coulton
context: Power credits discussion and criticism; his separate general preface sets out the series’ evidentiary policy. That preface is not her authorial statement.
works: General preface to Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

label: A. Hamilton Thompson
context: Provides transcripts/translations of Alnwick’s register and reads manuscript/proofs; Power uses documentary comparison in evaluating injunctions.
works: Alnwick register materials acknowledged and discussed in Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

label: R. Bin Wong
context: Compares Chinese and European economic/state trajectories, using and testing historical categories.
works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

label: Maxine Berg
context: Her study of older British manufactures provides a directly cited resource for Roy’s account of productivity and organization beyond spectacular inventions.
works: The Age of Manufactures, 1700–1820, second edition (1994),40, through Roy (1999),8/note12

label: Raúl Prebisch
context: Questions the international distribution of technical gains and proposes industrialization supported by trade and capital imports.
works: El desarrollo económico de la América Latina y algunos de sus principales problemas (1949), selected introduction

label: Aldo Leopold
context: Ecological observation and conservation ethics precede the field’s later consolidation; Cronon identifies a landscape-training model drawn from Leopold.
works: A Sand County Almanac (1949)

label: Ronald Inden
context: Guha uses his analysis of Orientalist representations to question deep ecology’s selective appropriation of Asian traditions.
works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), received in Guha (1989)

label: Peter Pesic
context: A named interlocutor in disputes about Bacon, experiment and domination of nature; this is a focused criticism, not a rejection of environmental history.
works: “Wrestling with Proteus” (1999), author abstract

label: Rita Felski
context: Fraser credits her counterpublic vocabulary alongside Spivak.
works: Beyond Feminist Aesthetics (1989), cited in Fraser note 22

label: Georg / György Lukács
context: History and Class Consciousness (1923), with its account of reification and of Marxism as method, is the standard precursor of critical theory. Lukács was not a member of the Institute, and his later positions diverge from it.
works: History and Class Consciousness (1923)

label: Siegfried Kracauer
context: Critic and essayist of the Frankfurt milieu, close to Adorno and Benjamin but never a member of the Institute. His microhistory context, where Ginzburg records a retrospective affinity, remains distinct.
works: Das Ornament der Masse (1963; essays from the 1920s)

label: Louis Althusser
context: Defends Lacan’s return to Freud while later qualifying culturalist overtones of his own reading. A philosophical intervention in Communist debates, not a clinical case study.
works: “Freud and Lacan” (written 1964; NLR 1969), public opening and editorial qualification

label: E. P. Thompson
context: A historical resource extended and criticized; not represented as adopting all later gender theories.
works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963)

label: Nira Yuval-Davis
context: Gender-specific contribution on national projects and membership; does not stand for every racial-formation approach.
works: Gender and Nation (1997)

label: Chandra Talpade Mohanty
context: Connects gender analysis to colonial power and differences among women.
works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

label: Judith Butler
context: Questions the production of feminist subjects and gender norms; performativity is not unrestricted personal choice.
works: Gender Trouble (1990)

label: Susan Stryker
context: A situated trans theoretical and performance intervention contests exclusion within collective identities; later historical books lie beyond this mapped period.
works: “My Words to Victor Frankenstein” (1994; performance 1993)

label: Hazel V. Carby
context: Black feminist historical inquiry questions universal models of family, dependence and womanhood.
works: “White Woman Listen!” (1982; later reprint consulted)

label: Alice Clark
context: Her inclusion of unpaid production is explicitly valued by Erickson alongside criticism.
works: Working Life of Women (1919); reception in Erickson’s introduction (1992)

label: Lise Vogel
context: Reworks Marxian categories for gender and production/reproduction of material life; the checked publisher description supports the project, with its detailed mechanism awaiting primary reading.
works: Marxism and the Oppression of Women (1983), publisher description

label: Carroll Smith-Rosenberg
context: Connects bodily and social relations in a feminist theoretical contribution explicitly acknowledged by Spiegel.
works: “The Body Politic,” in Elizabeth Weed, ed., Coming to Terms: Feminism, Theory, Politics (1989), p. 101 cited by Spiegel

label: Sandra Harding
context: Develops a feminist inquiry into socially situated knowing.
works: Whose Science? Whose Knowledge? (1991)

label: Francesca Bray
context: Connects gender history with everyday technologies in late imperial China.
works: Technology and Gender (1997)

label: Amanda Vickery
context: Critically tests a major gender-and-class interpretation against regional evidence.
works: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), especially 393–401

label: Kathleen Canning
context: Develops a feminist response to Scott’s treatment of experience and agency.
works: “Feminist History after the Linguistic Turn” (1994), 374–379

label: Orin Grant Libby
context: Uses local political boundaries and population distribution to examine ratification.
works: The Geographical Distribution of the Vote (1894)

label: James C. Malin
context: Links historical inquiry to ecological adaptation; Worster acknowledges this resource while disputing Malin’s Dust Bowl explanations.
works: “Ecology and History” (1950); “Dust Storms” (1946), through Worster (1986)

label: Cemal Kafadar
context: An Ottoman self-writing study mediates a Davis resource in Subrahmanyam’s questions about individualism.
works: “Self and Others: The Diary of a Dervish in Seventeenth Century Istanbul and First-person Narratives in Ottoman Literature” (1989), cited in Connected Histories740n13

label: Alfred Crosby
context: Ecological histories provide explicitly cited resources in Subrahmanyam’s account of connected changes.
works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); cited in Connected Histories738n10

label: Philip Curtin
context: Cross-cultural trade supplies a world-historical subject distinct from his quantitative reconstruction of the slave trade.
works: Cross-Cultural Trade in World History (1984), bibliography in Rethinking World History (1993); The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

label: Philip C. C. Huang
context: His household involution argument is disputed by Pomeranz; later criticism distinguishes rising output from returns to labor.
works: The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta,1350–1988 (1990), through Pomeranz (2000) and Huang’s2002 review

label: R. Bin Wong
context: Compares Chinese and European economic/state trajectories, using and testing historical categories.
works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

label: Leopold von Ranke
context: Provides an earlier comparison for historical individuality and the value of epochs. His theology and documentary practice differ from later philosophies; no backward influence is implied.
works: 1824 preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

label: G. W. F. Hegel
context: Marx retrospectively identifies critical reexamination of Hegel’s philosophy of law as a step toward his investigation of material relations. This is a specified critical resource, not adherence to the whole Hegelian system.
works: Philosophy of law, discussed in Marx’s 1859 preface

label: Gaetano Mosca
context: Political-class account discussed critically in Gramsci’s inquiry into intellectual functions.
works: Elementi di scienza politica (expanded edition1923), Gramsci author noteA

label: Vilfredo Pareto
context: An explicitly compared theorist; this selection does not imply Marxist affiliation.
works: Theory of elites, compared in Gramsci’s Intellectuals author noteA

label: Quintin Hoare
context: Editorial and translation work enables a particular English selection; translated history, education and politics.
works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

label: Geoffrey Nowell Smith
context: Translated intellectuals, Fordism and philosophy; editorial arrangement differs from notebook sequence.
works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

label: Erich Auerbach
context: White discusses representation through a comparison with literary inquiry.
works: Mimesis, cited by White in Metahistory (1973),2n1

label: Kathleen Canning
context: Develops a feminist response to Scott’s treatment of experience and agency.
works: “Feminist History after the Linguistic Turn” (1994), 374–379

label: Richard Rorty
context: Rorty’s anthology of analytic philosophers’ essays on philosophical method gave the phrase “the linguistic turn” wide currency. Historians’ linguistic turn drew mainly on other, often French, resources, so this records the name’s source, not a lineage.
works: The Linguistic Turn (1967), ed.

label: R. H. Tawney
context: External interlocutor: Dobb credits his rising-producer interpretation. The exact cited Tawney passage is unresolved; Christian socialism does not imply Marxist membership.
works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926); reception in Dobb’s 1950 reply

label: E. A. Kosminsky
context: Peasant research is a named resource in Dobb’s reply and Hilton’s later synthesis. The 1956 work is the Hilton context; it is not projected backward as a publication read by Dobb in 1950.
works: Studies in the Agrarian History of England in the Thirteenth Century (1956), cited by Hilton (1973); earlier peasant interpretation cited by Dobb (1950)

label: Frances James
context: Offers a specific Marxist review of Flexner; this selection identifies the argument in the review, not a fully researched career or universal Marxist position.
works: “Century of Women’s Struggle” (International Socialist Review, 1960)

label: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese
context: In the 1978 exchange she challenges Stone’s crisis/progress assumptions and defends Tuchman’s narrative interpretation, explicitly without assigning Tuchman to Marxism. This selection concerns that dated intervention.
works: Letter in “Tuchman and History” (7 December 1978)

label: Frances A. Yates
context: Mnemonic techniques and their historical transformations provide a comparison with social frameworks and commemoration, without a founding claim.
works: The Art of Memory (1966), preface and concluding chapter

label: Aby Warburg
context: Jan Assmann discusses Warburg with Halbwachs as an early theorist of social and cultural memory, alongside the Warburg Institute’s own account of his library. A precursor in Assmann’s account, not a founder of memory studies as a field.
works: Bilderatlas Mnemosyne (1924–29, unfinished)

label: Natalie Zemon Davis
context: The Return of Martin Guerre reconstructs a sixteenth-century village imposture case and is a standard example of microhistory in English. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.
works: The Return of Martin Guerre (1983)

label: Martin Broszat
context: Led the Institut für Zeitgeschichte’s Bayern in der NS-Zeit project, a founding programme for the history of everyday life under National Socialism. His structuralist interpretation of the regime is a separate context.
works: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–1983), ed. with others

label: Carl von Clausewitz
context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

label: Hans Delbrück
context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

label: Frantz Fanon
context: Distinguishes elite succession from popular emancipation.
works: The Wretched of the Earth (1961), “The Pitfalls of National Consciousness”

label: Prasenjit Duara
context: Questions linear national histories through competing local, national and transnational narratives.
works: Rescuing History from the Nation (1995)

label: C. V. Wedgwood
context: Connects verse and visual culture with political imagination. This extends cultural inquiry without establishing descent from Burckhardt or Huizinga.
works: Poetry and Politics under the Stuarts (1960)

label: Elizabeth Lapovsky Kennedy
context: Coauthor of a collaborative Buffalo lesbian oral history; differentiated local experiences inform the interpretation.
works: Boots of Leather, Slippers of Gold (1993)

label: Madeline D. Davis
context: Coauthor of a collaborative Buffalo lesbian oral history; differentiated local experiences inform the interpretation.
works: Boots of Leather, Slippers of Gold (1993)

label: Angela Cavender Wilson
context: Wahpetonwan Dakota historian argues for tribal and family historians’ authority, sustained relationships and careful interpretation of transmitted knowledge.
works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

label: Julie Cruikshank
context: Anthropologist and collaborator in a southern Yukon life-history project; the elders are knowledge producers, not anonymous source material. Her 1993 discussion paper examines how institutional settings reshape the interpretation of oral traditions.
works: Life Lived Like a Story, with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned (1990); Claiming Legitimacy (1993 draft discussion paper)

label: Angela Sidney
context: Named elder collaborator whose life narrative helps constitute the Yukon book; not merely a subject of an academic biography.
works: Life Lived Like a Story, collaborative volume (1990)

label: Kitty Smith
context: Named elder collaborator in the southern Yukon narrative project; her contribution is retained separately from the other narrators.
works: Life Lived Like a Story, collaborative volume (1990)

label: Annie Ned
context: Named elder collaborator in the southern Yukon narrative project; collaboration does not imply interchangeable experiences.
works: Life Lived Like a Story, collaborative volume (1990)

label: Silvia Rivera Cusicanqui
context: Her account of THOA emphasizes Aymara direction and collective discussion; the workshop’s knowledge is not her individual creation.
works: “El potencial epistemológico y teórico de la historia oral” (1987)

label: Alice Lynd
context: Coedits a selective organizer collection with explicit participant correction, combining interviews with written accounts and speeches.
works: With Staughton Lynd, eds., Rank and File (1973), introduction

label: Staughton Lynd
context: Coedits a selective organizer collection with explicit participant correction, combining interviews with written accounts and speeches.
works: With Alice Lynd, eds., Rank and File (1973), introduction

label: Betty Balanoff
context: Provides oral-history resources to the Lynds’ organizer-history project.
works: Resources acknowledged in Rank and File (1973)

label: Marc Bloch
context: Historian of evidence who distinguishes origins from explanation and treats traces as answers to questions under evidential constraints.
works: Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (1949)

label: Giambattista Vico
context: Michelet explicitly appropriates humanity’s self-making as a historical principle; original Vico is not read here.
works: Scienza nuova as recalled in Michelet (1869)

label: John Stuart Mill
context: A named resource against fixed innate explanations in Michelet’s account of historical formation.
works: Passage quoted by Michelet (1869), p. 142

label: Johann Gottfried Herder
context: Lamprecht credits a conception of collective historical life; this is a mediated resource, not a universal origin claim.
works: Ideas concerning the History of Mankind, as cited by Lamprecht (1905)

label: Leopold von Ranke
context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

label: Immanuel Kant
context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.

label: G. W. F. Hegel
context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

label: Friedrich Schleiermacher
context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

label: Frank Ramsey
context: Wittgenstein explicitly credits discussions in the last two years of Ramsey’s life. The selection records that acknowledgment, not a claim about a distinct historical method or an identified passage in Ramsey’s published work.
works: Discussions acknowledged in the January 1945 preface to Philosophical Investigations

label: Piero Sraffa
context: Wittgenstein credits sustained criticism with fruitful ideas. The preface supports an intellectual resource; it does not identify the criticism with all of Sraffa’s economic arguments.
works: Critical conversations acknowledged in the January 1945 preface to Philosophical Investigations

label: Garrett Mattingly
context: Mink uses a historical narrative as a test case for understanding despite already knowing its outcome.
works: The Defeat of the Spanish Armada, cited in Mink1970,546

label: George Santayana
context: Becker closes by citing history’s enlargement of experience; the quoted civilizational ranking is not endorsed.
works: The Life of Reason,V,68, quoted in Becker1931address

label: Margaret R. Somers
context: Studies citizenship as a historical process shaped by law, associational life and political culture in English communities.
works: “Citizenship and the Place of the Public Sphere” (1993)

label: James Epstein
context: Co-edits research on Chartism with Dorothy Thompson; a collection containing differing approaches does not establish agreement among all its contributors.
works: The Chartist Experience: Studies in Working-Class Radicalism and Culture, 1830–60 (co-editor with Dorothy Thompson, 1982)

label: Hubert Hall
context: Provides documentary training in Cam’s London formation.
works: Palaeographical and diplomatic training discussed in Cheney’s Cam memoir, p. 297

label: Hilary Jenkinson
context: Provides documentary training; no shared position on all archival questions is inferred.
works: Training discussed in Cheney’s Cam memoir, p. 297

label: C. R. Cheney
context: Appreciates Cam’s institutional inquiry while questioning some juristic deductions and broad accounts of legal progress.
works: “Helen Maud Cam, 1885–1968,” especially pp. 303–305

label: J. E. Neale
context: Advises on the structure of Wedgwood’s first Strafford biography.
works: Advice or scholarship discussed in Woolrych, pp. 523–524, concerning Strafford (1935) and its 1961 revaluation

label: J. P. Cooper
context: Scholarship contributes to Wedgwood’s revaluation of Strafford, according to Woolrych.
works: Advice or scholarship discussed in Woolrych, pp. 523–524, concerning Strafford (1935) and its 1961 revaluation

label: Hugh Kearney
context: Research contributes to the revised assessment; no identical position on every aspect is claimed.
works: Advice or scholarship discussed in Woolrych, pp. 523–524, concerning Strafford (1935) and its 1961 revaluation

label: Gerald Aylmer
context: Work contributes to a reassessment alongside new documentary access.
works: Advice or scholarship discussed in Woolrych, pp. 523–524, concerning Strafford (1935) and its 1961 revaluation

label: Gilman M. Ostrander

label: C. H. McIlwain

label: Quentin Skinner
context: Political texts as historically possible interventions, with social conditions and public conventions constraining interpretation.

label: J. G. A. Pocock
context: Political thinking at historically available levels and a selective inquiry into republican fragility, virtue and corruption.
works: Methodological inquiry (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975), introduction

label: Reinhart Koselleck
context: Political concepts as historical indicators and factors, with their social referents and temporal horizons remaining distinct objects of inquiry.

label: Graham Wallas
context: Namier explicitly takes up his inquiry into habitual and partly unconscious political thinking.
works: Human Nature in Politics (1908), discussed in Namier’s 1955 essay

label: Silvia Ratto
context: Goldman credits their earlier joint presentation on public opinion and the constituent congress.
works: “Opinión pública e ilustración en el Río de la Plata” (joint presentation, 1997), cited by Goldman (2000), note 26

label: Bernard S. Cohn
context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.

label: Gyan Prakash
context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.

label: Stuart Hall
context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.

label: Paul Gilroy
